Independent civic data project

Fiscal impact, corrected

Read the Town’s fiscal-impact statement next to a realistic financial interpretation — while separately checking whether the resolution was adopted, how members voted, and whether an official adopted-resolution document is available.

Independent project·Updated October 4, 2026·● Current·Check data freshness →
💡In plain English
Across 18 Town Board meetings in 2026, the Town marked 605 resolutions as having no fiscal impact — and on a realistic read, at least 221 of those plainly commit or change money. A second group is easy to miss: 124 resolutions the Town did mark as having an impact, but called absorbed by the existing budget, actually draw on reserves, fund balance or borrowing.
  • ›What the form is: a one-page checklist the Town attaches to each resolution: does it have a fiscal impact (yes/no), can it be “absorbed” by the current budget, and what’s the funding source.
  • ›What it does not prove: a fiscal-impact form is not proof that the resolution was finally adopted or that every member voted a particular way. The meeting record and any separately published adopted-resolution document answer those questions.
  • ›Why correct it: the checkbox answer is frequently “no” or “absorbed” even when the resolution commits real dollars — a new salary, a union settlement, a capital purchase, a fee change.
  • ›How we read it: the Town’s own Yes/No answer sits next to a plain-English realistic read keyed on the resolution’s category. Where the Town’s account codes or the resolution’s own words say more, they decide instead: closing a finished project commits no new money. Dollar figures are shown only where they can be tied to a source without guessing.
  • ›What the resolution states: under each title, every dollar figure in the resolution’s own text, quoted as printed and labelled: a cost, a fee paid to the Town, money coming in, the size of a grant program applied to, a budget-table line, borrowing, a developer’s security, or background. Insurance an applicant must carry is left out. Only a figure that reads as the Town paying out counts as a stated cost. Where the statement names less than the resolution’s own budget table moves, both figures are shown.

What the Town’s own accounting says

On 10 of this meeting’s 37 statements the preparer filled in section G with actual chart-of-accounts codes — the appropriation account to be charged, the revenue source, or an appropriation transfer. Those codes are matched below against the line items of the 2026 Adopted Budget, so the question stops being “does this cost money?” and becomes “which budget line, and how much of it?” On 6 of them the account code, not the resolution’s title, decides the read.

Of the 37 resolutions, 17 get a different answer here than the Town gave. 7 were marked no fiscal impact yet commit or change real money. Another 10 the Town did flag as having an impact, but called absorbed by the existing budget — on a realistic read those draw on reserves, fund balance or borrowing, which is not the same as costing nothing.

Source: Town of Riverhead Town Board Agenda Packet, 2026-09-15 (Fiscal Impact Statements). Each resolution's Town 'Fiscal Impact Statement' answer (Yes/No and absorbed vs. detailed) is transcribed as-published from the agenda packet, alongside a plain-English realistic read keyed on the resolution's category. The amount comes from section G of the statement, where the preparer wrote one. Where the budget table the Board adopted puts a different figure on a fund's Appropriated Fund Balance account, the table's figure is used, because the vote is the appropriation, and section G's is shown beside it. Separately, every dollar figure the resolution's own text states is listed and quoted, each labelled by its wording (a cost, a pay rate, a fee paid to the Town, a grant, a fund-balance transfer, a budget-adjustment line or background); insurance limits an applicant must carry are left out. The stated cost is the largest figure that reads as the Town paying out, taking what the Board resolves over the recitals. Where section G names less than the resolution's own budget table moves, both figures are shown. This is an independent read, not the Town’s official position. A fiscal-impact form documents the Town’s financial treatment of a proposed resolution; by itself it does not prove that the resolution was adopted or how each member voted. Verify against the agenda packet, minutes, and any separately published adopted-resolution document.

Why this matters for the budget

The items that follow the Town into future budgets are the recurring ones the form tends to wave through: new full-time and part-time hires, seasonal payroll, and union stipulations (CSEA, PBA, SOA), whose wage terms compound with each future budget. Those recurring commitments — not the one-time purchases — are what a resident should track against next year’s tax levy. See how they interact with the 2026 retirement buyout and the full meeting decision record.
